The Catholic historian Brad Gregory argues that the Reformation unintentionally fathered the fragmented, secularized, hyper-individual modern world, the world in which, once the final authority has been relocated into each believer's own reading, every person becomes in effect his own interpreter with no court above him (Gregory 2012). Give all of that its full weight. The downstream costs were real, and the Reformers did not foresee them.

And steel-man the secular reduction too, the account that says it was never really about theology. Yes, the printing press spread Luther's tracts faster than Rome could answer them. Yes, German princes had political and financial reasons to shield him from the emperor. Yes, nationalism and money were in the mix. The material factors were genuine. But they explain the speed of the fire, not the fire itself. Erasmus mocked the church's corruption more wittily than Luther ever did and started no reformation, because mockery of corruption is not a gospel. Luther had a gospel.

Now the reversal, the thing the modern reader assumes is behind us. People treat the Reformation as a five-hundred-year-old institutional quarrel the secular world has happily outgrown. It is the reverse. The question it raised is more alive now than it has ever been, because the modern self simply relocated the courtroom. You may no longer fear standing before God, but you stand every single day before some other tribunal, the market, the feed, the mirror, the endless audit of whether you are successful enough, attractive enough, productive enough, enough. Luther's anguish was not a medieval relic. It was the human condition, and the secular age did not cure it. It only removed the one verdict that could ever have silenced it. The performance treadmill is works-righteousness with God deleted, all of the judgment and none of the grace.

I am a Protestant pastor. I preach justification by faith, and I still live half my life on that treadmill, auditing my worth by the size of the crowd and the warmth of the reviews, which means I have heard Luther's discovery and not yet believed it all the way to the floor. The Reformation is not a date I celebrate once a year. It is a deliverance I need again every week.

Luther stood before the emperor at Worms in 1521 and was ordered to take it all back, and he answered that he could not, because his conscience was captive to the word of God. We remember the courage and forget the relief underneath it. He was not mainly being brave. He was being free, free the way only a man can be who has stopped trying to earn what he has finally learned is given. That freedom is still on offer, and the question that drove him to it is still the only question that finally matters about your life. Not whether you are enough. Whether you will receive the righteousness you could never manufacture. The Reformation was the rediscovery that the answer is yes, and that it costs you nothing, because it already cost God everything.

### Works Cited

Gregory, Brad S. 2012. The Unintended Reformation. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press.

McGrath, Alister E. 2005. Iustitia Dei: A History of the Christian Doctrine of Justification. 3rd ed. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Taylor, Charles. 2007. A Secular Age. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press.

chapters.title: Liturgical vs. Contemporary Worship: What We Gained and What We Lost
chapters.summary: The worship wars of the 1990s were never really about music. They were about what worship is for — and the answer to that question shapes what kind of Christians we become.
chapters.body:
Every Sunday, across tens of thousands of churches, two fundamentally different visions of Christian worship are enacted, often without their participants understanding the assumptions behind either one. In one church, a congregation stands and sits and kneels in choreographed rhythm, following a printed order of service that includes a call to worship, a confession of sin, a declaration of pardon, the reading of three Scripture lessons, a sermon tied to the lectionary, the recitation of the Nicene Creed, the celebration of the Eucharist, and a benediction. In the church down the road, a worship band opens with twenty minutes of singing, the congregation remains standing with hands raised, the pastor delivers a forty-five-minute topical sermon with video clips and personal stories, an altar call is given, and the service ends with a closing song.

Both of these are Christian worship. Both involve the reading of Scripture, prayer, singing, and preaching. But they are built on different foundations, shaped by different histories, and — most importantly — they form different kinds of Christians. The question of liturgical versus contemporary worship is not, at bottom, a question of preference. It is a question of formation: What is worship *for*, and what does it do to us over time?

## What Liturgy Actually Means

The word "liturgy" comes from the Greek *leitourgia*, which means "the work of the people." In ancient Athens, a liturgy was a public work performed by a wealthy citizen for the benefit of the community — funding a warship or sponsoring a festival. The early church adopted the term for its public worship, and the etymology is revealing: liturgy is not something performed by clergy for a passive audience. It is the common work of the gathered community, in which every person participates.

In its Christian usage, liturgy refers to a structured, repeating pattern of worship that follows a set order — an *ordo* — rooted in the practice of the early church. The basic shape of this pattern is remarkably consistent across traditions that practice liturgical worship (Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, and many Reformed and Methodist churches): *gathering* (the community assembles and is called to worship), *word* (Scripture is read and preached), *table* (the Eucharist is celebrated), and *sending* (the community is dismissed to serve in the world).

This fourfold pattern is not arbitrary. It can be traced to the worship of the second-century church, described in Justin Martyr's *First Apology* (c. 155 AD): "On the day called Sunday, all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place, and the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits; then, when the reader has ceased, the president verbally instructs, and exhorts to the imitation of these good things. Then we all rise together and pray." Justin goes on to describe the celebration of the Eucharist, with bread and wine consecrated by prayer and distributed to all present.

The liturgical tradition holds that this pattern — word and table, together, every week — is not merely one option among many but the normative pattern of Christian worship, established by the apostolic church and maintained across the centuries. Departure from this pattern is not innovation; it is impoverishment.

## The Rise of Contemporary Worship

The contemporary worship movement did not emerge from a vacuum. It was a response to genuine problems in the liturgical tradition as practiced in mid-twentieth-century American Protestantism. Mainline churches in the 1950s and 1960s were, in many cases, liturgically correct but spiritually moribund — going through the motions of worship without passion, conviction, or connection to the lives of ordinary people. The language of the liturgy was archaic, the music was inaccessible, the preaching was cerebral and detached, and the overall atmosphere was formal, reserved, and unwelcoming to outsiders.

The contemporary worship movement sought to address these failures by making worship accessible, emotionally engaging, and culturally relevant. Its roots are multiple: the Jesus Movement of the 1970s, which brought folk and rock music into worship; the Vineyard movement of the 1980s, which developed the "worship set" format of extended, emotionally building musical worship; the seeker-sensitive movement of the 1990s, pioneered by Willow Creek Community Church, which redesigned worship to remove barriers for unchurched visitors; and the global influence of Hillsong Church, which produced a stream of worship songs that became the de facto hymnody of evangelical Christianity worldwide.

What the contemporary movement gained was substantial. It made church accessible to millions of people who would never have crossed the threshold of a traditional church. It recovered the emotional dimension of worship — the sense that worship should involve the whole person, not just the intellect. It demonstrated that the gospel could be communicated in the cultural language of the present, not just the cultural language of the sixteenth or seventeenth century. It created a participatory atmosphere in which people felt free to express their devotion physically — through raised hands, through tears, through spontaneous prayer.

## What the Contemporary Movement Lost

But the gains came at a cost, and the cost has become increasingly visible as the contemporary movement has matured. Several losses deserve attention.

The first is *depth of content*. The hymns of the liturgical tradition — "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God," "O Sacred Head Now Wounded," "Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing" — are dense with theological content, drawing on centuries of doctrinal reflection. The average contemporary worship song is built on a much narrower theological range: God's love, God's greatness, the worshipper's response of praise. Studies of the most popular contemporary worship songs have found that they overwhelmingly focus on the subjective experience of the worshipper ("I will praise you," "You are good to me") rather than on the objective acts of God in history (creation, incarnation, crucifixion, resurrection, ascension, coming judgment). The effect, over time, is a congregation that knows how it feels about God but is less clear about who God is and what God has done.

The second loss is *continuity with the historic church*. When a congregation recites the Nicene Creed, it is saying the same words that Christians have said since 381 AD. When it follows the lectionary, it is reading the same passages that Christians around the world are reading on the same day. When it observes the church calendar — Advent, Christmas, Epiphany, Lent, Holy Week, Easter, Pentecost — it is living inside a narrative structure that shapes the entire year around the story of Christ. The contemporary worship movement, by and large, abandoned these connections. Most non-denominational churches do not follow a lectionary, do not observe the church calendar (beyond Christmas and Easter), do not recite the creeds, and do not celebrate the Eucharist weekly. The result is a form of worship that is cut off from the church's memory — a perpetual present tense with no sense of the centuries of faith that preceded it.

The third loss is *silence*. Liturgical worship includes structured moments of silence — after the Scripture readings, after the sermon, during the Eucharist — that create space for reflection, confession, and interior prayer. Contemporary worship tends to fill every moment with sound: the worship band plays continuously, the transitions are seamless, and the emotional arc of the service is carefully managed. The absence of silence is not accidental; it reflects a culture that is uncomfortable with stillness and a theology that associates God's presence with emotional intensity rather than with the "still small voice" of 1 Kings 19.

The fourth loss is *corporate identity*. Liturgical worship is, by design, communal. The congregation speaks together, sings together, confesses together, receives communion together. The individual is absorbed into the body. Contemporary worship, despite its communal setting, can be a surprisingly individualistic experience — a room full of people having private emotional encounters with God, mediated by music and lighting designed to create a particular mood. The shift from hymnals to projected lyrics is emblematic: the hymnal was a shared text that connected the congregation to each other and to a tradition; the projected lyric, appearing and disappearing on a screen, connects the individual to a momentary experience.

## The Worship Wars

The so-called "worship wars" of the 1990s and 2000s — the bitter conflicts within congregations over music style, instrumentation, and worship format — were never really about music. They were about two competing visions of what the church is and what worship is for. The liturgical vision holds that worship is the church's participation in the eternal worship of God — an objective reality that exists whether or not the worshippers feel anything. The contemporary vision holds that worship is the church's response to God's presence — an experience that should be felt, expressed, and emotionally authentic.

Both visions have biblical warrant. The Psalms include both liturgical instruction ("Lift up your heads, O gates") and emotional expression ("My soul thirsts for you"). The worship of Revelation is both highly liturgical (structured around hymns, acclamations, and ritual actions) and overwhelmingly experiential (the worshippers fall on their faces, cry out, and are consumed by the glory of God). The early church practiced both form and freedom, structure and spontaneity.

The worship wars were destructive not because the underlying questions were unimportant but because they were conducted without theological sophistication. Churches split over whether to use drums rather than over what worship is meant to accomplish in the lives of believers. The question of *formation* — what kind of people does this worship produce over a lifetime? — was rarely asked.

## Blended Worship: Compromise or Synthesis?

Many churches have attempted to resolve the tension through "blended worship" — services that combine elements of both traditions. A typical blended service might include a call to worship and a responsive reading (liturgical elements), followed by a set of contemporary worship songs, a topical sermon, and a closing hymn. Some churches offer separate services in different styles; others attempt to weave the traditions together in a single service.

The results are mixed. At its best, blended worship draws on the strengths of both traditions — the theological depth and historical continuity of the liturgical tradition, the accessibility and emotional authenticity of the contemporary tradition. At its worst, it satisfies no one — the liturgical elements feel perfunctory, the contemporary elements feel shoehorned in, and the overall experience is incoherent rather than integrated.

The most successful examples of blended worship tend to be those that begin with the liturgical *ordo* — gathering, word, table, sending — and express it in contemporary musical and cultural language, rather than those that begin with a contemporary framework and insert liturgical elements as decoration.

## Why Young People Are Returning to Liturgy

One of the more striking trends in American Christianity over the past decade has been the movement of young adults — particularly those raised in contemporary evangelical churches — toward liturgical traditions: Anglicanism, Catholicism, Orthodoxy, and liturgical expressions of Lutheranism and Presbyterianism. The trend is not statistically enormous, but it is culturally significant, and it has generated a substantial body of personal testimony and sociological analysis.

The reasons are multiple. Young people raised on contemporary worship often report a hunger for depth, substance, and historical rootedness that their experience of Christianity did not provide. They want to be connected to something older than last week's sermon series. They want a worship experience that does not depend on the charisma of the lead pastor or the quality of the worship band. They want structured silence in a world of constant noise. They want the Eucharist — the physical act of receiving the body and blood of Christ — rather than the monthly or quarterly memorial meal that many contemporary churches offer.

There is also a generational factor. Millennials and Gen Z have grown up in a culture saturated with commercial entertainment, and they are often the first to recognize when worship has become indistinguishable from a concert. The aesthetic of the contemporary megachurch — the fog machines, the light shows, the high production values — can feel, to a generation weary of being marketed to, less like worship and more like another consumer experience.

## Evaluating Worship by Formation, Not Preference

The most productive way to evaluate any worship practice is to ask not "Do I like it?" but "What is it doing to me?" Worship is not entertainment. It is not self-expression. It is, in the deepest sense, *formation* — the slow, repetitive, often unconscious process by which a community is shaped into a particular kind of people. The question is not whether the music is good or the sermon is interesting. The question is: Over a lifetime of participation, what kind of Christian will this worship produce?

A worship practice that never exposes the congregation to the full narrative arc of Scripture — creation, fall, redemption, consummation — will produce Christians with a truncated understanding of the faith. A worship practice that never includes corporate confession of sin will produce Christians who are unaware of their own brokenness. A worship practice that never celebrates the Eucharist will produce Christians who are disconnected from the central act of Christian worship for the first nineteen centuries of the church's existence. A worship practice that never makes space for silence will produce Christians who cannot hear the voice of God apart from amplified music.

Conversely, a worship practice that is all form and no feeling will produce Christians who can recite the creed but have never been moved by it. A worship practice that refuses to engage the culture will produce a church that talks only to itself. The goal is not to choose one tradition over the other but to ask, honestly and courageously, whether the worship we practice is forming us into the people God intends us to be — or merely confirming us in the preferences we already have.

chapters.title: Pentecostalism and the Global South
chapters.summary: The most significant development in global Christianity over the past century is not a new theology, a papal encyclical, or a denominational merger. It is the explosive growth of Pentecostalism in the Global South, a movement that has redrawn the map of world Christianity and challenged every assumption Western Christians hold about what the faith looks like.
chapters.body:
On April 9, 1906, in a converted stable at 312 Azusa Street in Los Angeles, something happened that would reshape global Christianity more profoundly than any event since the Reformation. A small group of worshippers, led by William J. Seymour, a one-eyed Black preacher and the son of former slaves, began speaking in tongues, a phenomenon they identified as the baptism of the Holy Spirit described in Acts 2. The Azusa Street Revival would continue for three years, drawing visitors from around the world who carried its fire back to their home countries. Within a century, the movement it spawned would claim over 600 million adherents worldwide, making Pentecostalism the fastest-growing form of Christianity in human history.

The irony is worth pausing over. The movement that would become the dominant expression of twenty-first-century Christianity was born not in a cathedral or a university but in a former horse stable. It was led not by a credentialed theologian but by a man denied admission to the seminary of his own denomination because of his race. And it was, in its earliest expression, radically interracial, a fact that would be quickly suppressed as American racial ideology reasserted itself.

## Azusa Street: The Interracial Origins

William Joseph Seymour (1870-1922) was born in Centerville, Louisiana, to parents who had been enslaved. He was largely self-educated, having been denied formal theological training by Charles Fox Parham's Bible school in Houston, which allowed him to listen to lectures only from the hallway because of his race. Seymour took Parham's teaching on the baptism of the Holy Spirit and transformed it into something Parham never intended: an interracial, egalitarian, Spirit-filled community that violated every social convention of early twentieth-century America.

The Azusa Street Mission was remarkable not only for its spiritual phenomena, speaking in tongues, healings, prophecies, but for its social composition. Black, white, Latino, and Asian worshippers prayed, sang, and fell under the Spirit together in an era when such mixing was both illegal in some jurisdictions and unthinkable in most churches. Frank Bartleman, a white eyewitness, famously wrote that at Azusa Street "the color line was washed away in the blood." This was an overstatement, the racial dynamics were more complex than hagiography suggests, but the aspiration was genuine and the reality, however imperfect, was extraordinary for its time.

The interracial character of early Pentecostalism did not survive. By 1914, when the Assemblies of God was organized as a predominantly white denomination, the movement had already segregated along racial lines. The Church of God in Christ, led by Charles Harrison Mason, became the largest Black Pentecostal denomination. The racial divide in American Pentecostalism mirrored the racial divide in American Christianity more broadly, a failure that haunts the movement to this day.

## The Four Waves

Scholars of Pentecostalism typically identify four waves or phases of the movement. The first wave is **classical Pentecostalism**, the denominational tradition that emerged directly from Azusa Street and its precursors. This includes the Assemblies of God, the Church of God in Christ, the Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee), the International Church of the Foursquare Gospel (founded by Aimee Semple McPherson), and numerous smaller bodies. These denominations are characterized by a distinct theology of "subsequence": the baptism of the Holy Spirit is understood as an experience subsequent to and distinct from conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues.

The second wave is the **charismatic renewal** movement that emerged in the 1960s and 1970s within mainline Protestant and Roman Catholic churches. Episcopal priest Dennis Bennett's 1960 announcement that he had received the gift of tongues is often cited as the beginning of the charismatic movement in mainline Protestantism. The Catholic Charismatic Renewal, which began at Duquesne University in 1967, eventually claimed tens of millions of adherents worldwide. These movements adopted Pentecostal spiritual practices while remaining within their existing denominational structures.

The third wave, identified by C. Peter Wagner in the 1980s, encompasses **neo-charismatic** movements that emphasize signs and wonders, spiritual warfare, and the continuation of apostolic gifts but do not necessarily identify as Pentecostal or charismatic. The Vineyard movement, founded by John Wimber, is a prominent example. The fourth and most consequential wave consists of **independent and indigenous** Pentecostal-type movements in the Global South that have no organizational connection to Western Pentecostal denominations but share their emphasis on the immediate experience of the Holy Spirit, healing, deliverance, and exuberant worship.

## The Explosive Growth

The numbers are staggering. In 1900, there were essentially no Pentecostals. By 1970, the combined Pentecostal and charismatic movement numbered perhaps 70 million. By 2000, estimates ranged from 400 to 500 million. By 2025, the number exceeds 600 million by most scholarly estimates, with some projections suggesting it could reach 800 million or more by mid-century. If Pentecostal and charismatic Christians were a single denomination, they would constitute the second-largest Christian tradition in the world, behind only Roman Catholicism.

The growth is concentrated overwhelmingly in the Global South. In Latin America, Pentecostalism has transformed the religious landscape. Brazil alone has an estimated 50 to 60 million Pentecostals, and the proportion continues to grow. Guatemala has become majority Protestant, primarily Pentecostal. Chile, Argentina, Colombia, and Mexico have experienced massive Pentecostal growth. In sub-Saharan Africa, Pentecostal and charismatic churches have exploded across the continent, from Nigeria (where the Redeemed Christian Church of God claims over 10 million members) to South Africa, Kenya, Ghana, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. In East Asia, the world's largest congregation, Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul, South Korea, is Pentecostal, with a membership that has exceeded 800,000.

## Why Pentecostalism Grows

Multiple explanations have been offered for this extraordinary growth, and no single factor suffices. But several recur across contexts and scholarly analyses.

First, Pentecostalism prioritizes **experience over doctrine**. One need not understand Trinitarian theology or be able to parse the Nicene Creed to receive the Holy Spirit. Pentecostal worship is participatory, emotional, and immediately accessible. You do not need literacy to speak in tongues, clap your hands, or be healed. In communities where formal education is limited, this accessibility is enormous.

Second, Pentecostalism takes the **spirit world seriously**. In much of the Global South, people live in what scholars call an "enchanted" worldview, one in which spiritual forces, both benign and malevolent, are understood as real and active. Western Christianity, shaped by the Enlightenment, has largely demythologized the spirit world. Pentecostalism has not. It offers prayer for healing, deliverance from demons, and spiritual power in a world where these categories are experientially real to millions of people. It meets people where they are rather than asking them to adopt a Western rationalist framework as a prerequisite for faith.

Third, Pentecostalism builds **community and mutual support networks** that function as social safety nets in contexts where the state provides little. Pentecostal churches often provide the same services that the Black church provided in the United States: education, economic assistance, healthcare, counseling, and a sense of belonging. For the urban poor migrating from rural areas to megacities like Lagos, Sao Paulo, or Manila, the Pentecostal church offers an instant community, a social network, and a moral framework for navigating a disorienting new environment.

Fourth, Pentecostalism is **indigenously adaptable**. Unlike Western missionary Christianity, which often came packaged with European cultural forms, liturgies, hymn tunes, architectural styles, and hierarchical structures, Pentecostalism adapts readily to local cultures. Its worship can incorporate local musical traditions, its leadership structures are often flat and entrepreneurial, and its theology, while maintaining certain core commitments, is flexible enough to be reinterpreted in radically different cultural contexts.

## Women and Pentecostalism

One of the most significant and underexamined dimensions of Pentecostal growth is the role of women. In many Global South contexts, Pentecostal conversion transforms gender dynamics within families and communities. The emphasis on sobriety, marital fidelity, and male domestic responsibility, values enforced by the Pentecostal community, often benefits women directly. Men who convert to Pentecostalism typically stop drinking, stop womanizing, and redirect income toward the household. The anthropologist Elizabeth Brusco, studying Colombian Pentecostals, described this as a "reformation of machismo" that empowered women even within a formally patriarchal theological framework.

Pentecostalism has also, paradoxically, provided women with public leadership roles that traditional churches denied them. The doctrine that the Holy Spirit distributes gifts without regard to gender has, in practice if not always in theory, opened space for women to preach, prophesy, plant churches, and lead ministries. Aimee Semple McPherson, who founded the International Church of the Foursquare Gospel in 1923, was one of the most famous religious leaders in American history, male or female. In the Global South, women serve as pastors, evangelists, and denominational leaders in numbers that would astonish observers accustomed to the gender hierarchies of traditional Christianity. The Spirit, it turns out, is a more effective feminist than any theological argument.

## David Martin's Thesis

The British sociologist David Martin, in his influential 2002 study *Pentecostalism: The World Their Parish*, argued that Pentecostalism represents the completion of a Reformation that classical Protestantism left unfinished. Luther and Calvin democratized theology, taking it out of the exclusive hands of the priestly caste and making it available to the literate layperson. But they still required literacy, education, and engagement with complex doctrinal systems. Pentecostalism goes further: it democratizes the experience of God itself, making the divine available to anyone, regardless of education, social status, or theological training.

Martin also argued that Pentecostalism functions as a form of cultural modernization, providing converts with the discipline, sobriety, mutual accountability, and work ethic that Max Weber associated with the "Protestant ethic." In Latin America especially, Pentecostal conversion often correlates with the abandonment of alcohol, the stabilization of family life, the development of small business, and upward economic mobility. This does not mean Pentecostalism is merely a vehicle for capitalist self-improvement, but the social effects are real and documented.

## The Tension: Spiritual Power and Theological Thinness

The strengths of Pentecostalism are inseparable from its vulnerabilities. The same emphasis on experience that makes the movement accessible also makes it susceptible to manipulation. If the Holy Spirit is the primary authority, and if discerning the Spirit is a subjective exercise, then the potential for charismatic leaders to claim divine sanction for personal agendas is immense. The history of Pentecostalism is littered with scandals, authoritarianism, and financial exploitation by leaders who claimed to speak for God.

The theological thinness of much Pentecostal Christianity is a genuine concern. The movement has produced relatively few systematic theologians, relatively little sustained engagement with historical Christian thought, and relatively weak institutional checks on doctrinal innovation. This has allowed prosperity theology, dominion theology, and various forms of spiritual entrepreneurialism to flourish under the Pentecostal umbrella. When the primary criterion for truth is "the Spirit told me," the tradition lacks internal mechanisms for self-correction.

## Prosperity Theology and the Global South

The prosperity gospel has found extraordinarily fertile ground in the Global South, and the picture is more complex than Western critics typically acknowledge. In contexts of extreme poverty, the message that God wants you to prosper is not merely a self-help gimmick. It is a radical theological claim that poverty is not God's will, that the faithful deserve dignity and material sufficiency, and that spiritual power can overcome structural disadvantage. The theology is often exegetically indefensible, its promises frequently unfulfilled, and its effects sometimes devastating when families give their last resources to prosperity preachers. But the appeal is rooted in real suffering and real hope.

The most problematic expressions of prosperity theology in the Global South involve leaders who live in spectacular wealth while their congregations remain impoverished. Churches that function as extraction mechanisms, demanding tithes and "seed offerings" from people who cannot afford them, represent a genuine form of spiritual exploitation. The challenge for Global South Pentecostalism is developing theological resources to critique prosperity theology from within, without dismissing the legitimate aspirations of the poor.

## Pentecostalism and Politics

The political dimensions of Pentecostal growth in the Global South deserve separate attention. In Brazil, the "bancada evangelica," the evangelical caucus in the national congress, has become one of the most powerful political blocs in the country. Pentecostal churches have elected mayors, governors, and senators across Latin America. In Nigeria, Pentecostal leaders wield enormous political influence. In Guatemala, two Pentecostal generals have served as president. The pattern is strikingly similar to the American evangelical trajectory: a movement that begins as spiritual renewal eventually discovers the utility of political power.

The consequences are complex. Pentecostal political engagement in the Global South has sometimes been prophetic, challenging corruption and advocating for the poor. It has also sometimes been reactionary, supporting authoritarian leaders, opposing LGBT rights, and aligning with economic elites whose interests are directly opposed to those of the Pentecostal faithful. The Brazilian election of Jair Bolsonaro in 2018, supported overwhelmingly by Pentecostal voters, echoed the American evangelical embrace of Donald Trump in ways that scholars are still analyzing. The question of whether Pentecostalism can sustain its prophetic energy while wielding political power is not yet answered.

## What Western Christianity Must Learn

The growth of Pentecostalism in the Global South presents Western Christianity with an uncomfortable mirror. It reveals the degree to which Western theology has been shaped by Enlightenment rationalism, how thoroughly Western worship has been domesticated by bourgeois respectability, and how completely Western ecclesiology has been captured by institutional maintenance.

Global South Christianity reminds the West that the Bible is an enchanted book, full of miracles, visions, healings, demons, and divine interventions that Western Christians have quietly demythologized or explained away. It reminds the West that worship is a full-body experience, not merely a cognitive one. It reminds the West that the church grows not through institutional efficiency but through the contagion of transformed lives.

This does not mean that Western Christians should uncritically adopt Global South forms. The theological weaknesses of much Pentecostalism are real. The susceptibility to prosperity theology is real. The authoritarianism is real. But the vitality is also real, and a Western Christianity that cannot account for why 600 million people have embraced this form of faith has something significant to learn about its own limitations.

## The Future Is Not Western

The demographic center of global Christianity has already shifted. By 2050, the majority of the world's Christians will live in Africa, Latin America, and Asia. The typical Christian will not be a white, middle-class American sitting in a suburban church. She will be a young woman in Lagos or Sao Paulo or Manila, worshipping in a Pentecostal church with loud music, fervent prayer, and an expectation that the Holy Spirit is present and active. She may not be able to explain the doctrine of the Trinity, but she can testify to what God has done in her life. She may not have read Karl Barth, but she has read the book of Acts and believes it describes normative Christianity rather than a historical curiosity.

The future of Christianity is not Western, not white, and not academic. This is not a prediction. It is a demographic reality. The question is whether Western Christians can receive this shift with humility, learning from traditions they have historically patronized, or whether they will cling to the assumption that real Christianity looks like what they have always known. The Spirit, it seems, has a preference for the margins.

chapters.title: The Anabaptist Option
chapters.summary: They rejected the state church, practiced believer's baptism, and insisted on nonviolence. Both Catholics and Protestants killed them for it. Four hundred years later, their ideas are more relevant than ever.
chapters.body:
In January 1525, a small group of men gathered in the home of Felix Manz in Zurich. They had been followers of Ulrich Zwingli, the city's reformer, but had grown convinced that Zwingli's reformation had not gone far enough. Zwingli had broken with Rome, but he had not broken with the fundamental assumption that had governed Christianity since Constantine: that the church and the state were bound together, that every citizen was a church member, and that infant baptism was the rite of entry into both civic and spiritual life.

That evening, Conrad Grebel baptized George Blaurock — an adult who had already been baptized as an infant. It was an act of profound theological significance and extraordinary political danger. By rebaptizing an adult, these men were not merely making a statement about the proper subjects of baptism. They were rejecting the entire Christendom model. They were saying that the church was not a territorial institution coextensive with the state but a voluntary community of committed believers. They were saying that faith could not be inherited, imposed, or assumed — it had to be chosen.

For this, they would be hunted, imprisoned, tortured, and killed — not only by Catholics, but by the very Protestants whose reformation they believed they were completing.

## The Radical Wing of the Reformation

The term "Anabaptist" — from the Greek *anabaptizo*, meaning "to baptize again" — was not a name these groups chose for themselves. It was a label applied by their enemies, and it carried legal weight. The Justinian Code, still in force across much of Europe, prescribed the death penalty for rebaptism. To call someone an Anabaptist was not merely to describe their theology; it was to mark them as criminals.

The Anabaptists were the radical wing of the Reformation — "radical" in the etymological sense of *radix*, root. Where Luther and Calvin sought to reform the existing church-state system, the Anabaptists sought to uproot it entirely. Their vision was not of a reformed Christendom but of a restored New Testament church — a community of voluntary, committed disciples who followed Jesus in all things, including his refusal to exercise coercive power.

This vision brought them into conflict with virtually every established authority in Europe. Catholics opposed them because they rejected the sacramental system, the papacy, and the entire institutional structure of the medieval church. Protestants opposed them because they rejected the state church, refused to bear arms, and denied that civil magistrates had any authority in matters of faith. The Anabaptists were, in the sixteenth century, a church without a country — and almost every country wanted them dead.

## The Schleitheim Confession

The clearest early statement of Anabaptist belief is the Schleitheim Confession of 1527, drafted primarily by Michael Sattler, a former Benedictine prior who had left the monastery to join the radical movement. The confession addressed seven articles, each of which represented a fundamental break with the Christendom model.

On baptism, the confession insisted that baptism was for believers only — for those who had "learned repentance and amendment of life" and who walked "in the resurrection of Jesus Christ." Infant baptism was "the highest and chief abomination of the pope," not because babies were unimportant, but because baptism without conscious faith was meaningless.

On the ban (church discipline), the confession established that unrepentant sinners were to be admonished and, if necessary, excluded from the fellowship. This was a corollary of believer's baptism: if membership was voluntary and meaningful, then the community had the right and responsibility to maintain its integrity.

On the sword, the confession was unequivocal: the use of violence was "outside the perfection of Christ." Christians were not to serve as magistrates, bear arms, or participate in the coercive functions of the state. "The rule of government is according to the flesh," the confession stated, "but the Christians' is according to the spirit." This was not merely a personal ethic of nonviolence; it was a comprehensive rejection of the idea that Christians could exercise lethal authority over others.

On the oath, the confession forbade swearing, following a literal reading of Jesus's command in Matthew 5:34-37. In a society where oaths undergirded the entire feudal system — oaths of allegiance, oaths of office, oaths in court — the refusal to swear was an act of social subversion. It marked the Anabaptists as people who stood outside the normal structures of social obligation.

Michael Sattler was arrested, tried, and executed three months after drafting the confession. His tongue was cut out, pieces of flesh were torn from his body with red-hot tongs, and he was burned at the stake. His wife, Margaretha, was drowned eight days later.

## Believer's Baptism and Its Political Implications

The Anabaptist insistence on believer's baptism was not, at its core, a dispute about the proper age for a ritual. It was a challenge to the fundamental political theology of Christendom. In the medieval and early modern world, infant baptism was simultaneously a religious sacrament and a civic registration. To be baptized was to become a member of both the church and the commonwealth. The parish register and the civil register were the same document. Church membership and citizenship were coextensive.

By insisting that baptism required conscious faith, the Anabaptists were effectively arguing for the separation of church and state — though they would not have used that phrase. They were saying that the church was a distinct community with its own criteria for membership, separate from the political community. A person could be a citizen without being a Christian, and a Christian without being a citizen of any particular state. This was, in the sixteenth century, a revolutionary idea, and the authorities treated it as such.

## The Munster Rebellion: The Disaster

The greatest catastrophe in Anabaptist history was the Munster Rebellion of 1534-1535, and its shadow fell over the entire movement for centuries. A group of radical Anabaptists, led by Jan Matthys and later by Jan van Leiden, seized control of the city of Munster in Westphalia, expelled all non-Anabaptists, established a theocratic regime, introduced polygamy, and proclaimed the city to be the New Jerusalem.

The bishop of Munster besieged the city. After sixteen months of increasingly desperate resistance — during which van Leiden crowned himself king, took multiple wives, and had dissenters executed — the city fell. The leaders were captured, tortured with red-hot tongs, and killed. Their bodies were displayed in iron cages hung from the steeple of St. Lambert's Church, where the cages remain to this day.

Munster was a genuine disaster, but it was wildly unrepresentative of the broader Anabaptist movement. The mainstream Anabaptists — the Swiss Brethren, the Hutterites, and the followers of Menno Simons — had no more in common with the Munster radicals than mainstream Muslims have in common with ISIS. They condemned the rebellion, reaffirmed their commitment to nonviolence, and suffered the consequences as authorities across Europe used Munster as justification for intensified persecution of all Anabaptists.

## Persecution from All Sides

The Anabaptists hold the grim distinction of being the only major Christian group persecuted by both Catholics and Protestants. In Catholic territories, they were hunted as heretics. In Protestant territories, they were prosecuted as seditionists and disturbers of the peace. Zwingli, who had once been sympathetic to the radicals, endorsed their execution by drowning — a grim irony given their views on baptism. Luther called them "Schwarmer" (fanatics) and supported their suppression. Calvin's Geneva was as hostile to Anabaptists as any Catholic court.

The Martyrs Mirror, compiled by Thieleman van Braght in 1660, records the stories of thousands of Anabaptist martyrs. It is one of the most harrowing documents in Christian history — a catalog of burnings, drownings, beheadings, and tortures that rivals the accounts of the early church's persecution under Rome. The Anabaptists understood their suffering in precisely those terms: they were the true heirs of the pre-Constantinian church, and their persecution proved it.

## Menno Simons and the Consolidation of the Movement

After the Munster debacle, the survival and rehabilitation of the Anabaptist movement owed more to Menno Simons than to any other individual. Simons, a former Catholic priest from Friesland, joined the Anabaptists in 1536 and spent the remaining quarter-century of his life organizing, teaching, and writing — always on the move, always in danger, always one step ahead of the authorities who had placed a bounty on his head.

Simons's theology was marked by three emphases: discipleship as the essence of the Christian life, the church as a visible community of committed believers, and nonresistance as the way of Christ. His followers — the Mennonites — became the largest and most enduring Anabaptist group, establishing communities across the Netherlands, Germany, Prussia, and eventually North America.

Simons's greatest contribution may have been his insistence that the Anabaptist vision was compatible with social stability. After Munster, Anabaptism was synonymous in the public mind with fanaticism and violence. Simons demonstrated, through decades of quiet, disciplined pastoral work, that a community could reject the state church, practice believer's baptism, and refuse to bear arms without descending into chaos. The Mennonite communities were, in fact, models of social order — industrious, honest, and self-governing. They survived not by seizing power but by rendering themselves useful to the societies around them.

## The Amish, the Hutterites, and the Brethren

The Anabaptist movement produced several distinct communities, each embodying the shared vision in its own way. The Amish, who split from the Mennonites in 1693 under the leadership of Jakob Ammann, practiced a particularly rigorous form of community discipline and separation from the world — the *Ordnung* that still governs Amish life today. The Hutterites, founded by Jakob Hutter in Moravia in the 1530s, practiced the community of goods — a literal communism rooted in the example of the Jerusalem church in Acts 2 and 4. The Church of the Brethren, founded in Germany in 1708, combined Anabaptist principles with Pietist spirituality.

What these groups shared was more significant than what divided them: a commitment to the voluntary church, to nonviolence, to simplicity of life, and to the conviction that following Jesus meant something concrete and costly — not merely believing the right doctrines but living in a particular way.

## Why the Anabaptist Vision Is Having a Renaissance

For most of the five centuries since their founding, the Anabaptists were a footnote in church history — a curiosity, a cautionary tale, or (in the case of the Amish) a tourist attraction. In the last several decades, however, the Anabaptist vision has experienced a remarkable revival, and it is not difficult to see why.

The collapse of Christendom — the end of the era in which Christianity enjoyed cultural dominance in the West — has made the Anabaptist critique of the state church newly relevant. As Western Christians find themselves increasingly in a post-Christian culture, the Anabaptist insistence that the church is a countercultural community of voluntary commitment rather than a cultural institution sustained by social convention sounds less like sectarian withdrawal and more like prophetic realism.

The theologian Stanley Hauerwas, arguably the most influential Christian ethicist of the late twentieth century, has drawn extensively on the Anabaptist tradition, arguing that the church's primary political task is not to make the state more Christian but to be the church — a community that embodies an alternative politics rooted in the Sermon on the Mount. Shane Claiborne and the New Monasticism movement have attempted to live out Anabaptist principles in urban settings, practicing radical hospitality, community of goods, and active peacemaking. Greg Boyd's *The Myth of a Christian Nation* is, in essence, an Anabaptist critique of American civil religion.

> The Anabaptists were four hundred years early. They argued for the separation of church and state when the idea seemed insane. They practiced nonviolence in a century of religious war. They insisted on voluntary faith in a world of coerced conformity. They were killed for these convictions by the thousands. And now, as Christendom crumbles and Christians across the West confront the question of how to be faithful in a culture that no longer supports their faith, the Anabaptist answer — be the church, not the empire — sounds less like a sectarian retreat and more like the only viable path forward.

This does not mean the Anabaptist tradition is without problems. Its tendencies toward insularity, its occasional legalism, its historical difficulty in engaging constructively with the broader culture — these are real limitations. But the core Anabaptist insight — that the church is most faithful not when it wields power but when it embodies an alternative — is one that the entire Christian tradition needs to hear, and needs to hear now more than ever.

chapters.title: The Charismatic Movement Inside Every Denomination
chapters.summary: The movement that began in a converted stable in Los Angeles in 1906 has now touched every branch of Christianity on earth. Its story is more complicated, more consequential, and more ambiguous than either its champions or its critics admit.
chapters.body:
In 1960, Dennis Bennett, the rector of St. Mark's Episcopal Church in Van Nuys, California, stood before his congregation and announced that he had received the baptism of the Holy Spirit and spoken in tongues. The announcement produced an immediate crisis. Some parishioners walked out. The local bishop asked Bennett to resign. The story made national news — not because speaking in tongues was new (Pentecostals had been doing it for half a century) but because Bennett was not a Pentecostal. He was an Episcopalian, a mainline Protestant, a man in a clerical collar with a graduate degree. The Holy Spirit, it seemed, had crossed a social boundary that American Christianity thought was firmly established.

Bennett's experience was not an isolated event. It was the opening act of a movement that would, over the next six decades, penetrate every major Christian tradition on earth — Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist — and reshape the landscape of global Christianity in ways that are still unfolding. The charismatic movement is, by virtually any measure, the most significant development in Christianity since the Reformation. Understanding it requires understanding its three distinct waves, its theological claims, its extraordinary gifts, and its equally extraordinary dangers.

## The First Wave: Classical Pentecostalism (1901-1960)

The origins of Pentecostalism are conventionally traced to January 1, 1901, when Agnes Ozman, a student at Charles Parham's Bethel Bible School in Topeka, Kansas, reportedly spoke in tongues after Parham laid hands on her and prayed. Parham, a former Methodist minister, had been studying the book of Acts and had concluded that the "initial evidence" of baptism in the Holy Spirit was speaking in tongues — a doctrine that would become the defining distinctive of classical Pentecostalism.

But it was the Azusa Street Revival of 1906-1909, led by William Seymour, an African American Holiness preacher and former student of Parham, that transformed Pentecostalism from a local curiosity into a global movement. Seymour established a mission in a converted stable at 312 Azusa Street in Los Angeles, and for three years, services ran almost continuously — morning, afternoon, and night — characterized by speaking in tongues, prophetic utterances, healings, and what participants described as overwhelming encounters with the presence of God.

The Azusa Street Revival was remarkable for several reasons beyond its pneumatological claims. It was radically interracial at a time when American society was rigidly segregated. Frank Bartleman, a white journalist who covered the revival, wrote, "The color line was washed away in the blood." Black, white, Hispanic, and Asian worshippers prayed together, laid hands on each other, and shared leadership in ways that were extraordinary for 1906 Los Angeles — or for most of American Christianity a century later. This interracial character was not incidental to the movement's theology; Seymour understood the crossing of racial boundaries as itself a sign of the Spirit's work, a fulfillment of the Pentecost narrative in which the Spirit was poured out "on all flesh."

The interracial unity did not last. Within a decade, the Pentecostal movement had largely segregated along racial lines, producing separate denominational structures for black and white believers. The Assemblies of God, founded in 1914, was predominantly white. The Church of God in Christ, which had actually predated the Assemblies of God as an organized body, became the primary African American Pentecostal denomination. The racial division of the movement was one of its earliest and most consequential failures — a failure that Pentecostal historians have increasingly confronted with candor.

Classical Pentecostalism established several theological distinctives that would shape all subsequent waves: the doctrine of baptism in the Holy Spirit as a distinct, post-conversion experience; the expectation of speaking in tongues as the initial evidence of this baptism; the continued operation of all the gifts of the Spirit described in the New Testament (prophecy, healing, miracles, discernment of spirits); and an eschatological urgency rooted in the conviction that the outpouring of the Spirit was a sign of the last days.

## The Second Wave: Charismatic Renewal (1960s-1980s)

Dennis Bennett's 1960 announcement marked the beginning of what historians call the charismatic renewal — the penetration of Pentecostal experience into the mainline Protestant and Catholic churches. The distinction between "Pentecostal" and "charismatic" is significant: Pentecostals left (or were expelled from) their existing denominations and formed new ones. Charismatics, by contrast, remained within their denominations, seeking to renew them from within.

The charismatic renewal spread with remarkable speed across denominational lines. By the mid-1960s, there were charismatic prayer groups and renewal movements among Episcopalians, Lutherans, Presbyterians, and Methodists. The movement attracted both clergy and laity, and it produced a substantial body of theological reflection that attempted to integrate charismatic experience with the doctrinal traditions of the host denominations.

The most significant — and to many observers, the most surprising — development was the emergence of the Catholic charismatic renewal. In February 1967, a group of faculty and students at Duquesne University in Pittsburgh attended a retreat during which several participants reported being baptized in the Holy Spirit and speaking in tongues. The movement spread rapidly to the University of Notre Dame and the University of Michigan, and within a decade, it had become one of the largest movements in the Catholic Church, with millions of participants worldwide.

The Catholic charismatic renewal was theologically distinctive in ways that set it apart from both classical Pentecostalism and Protestant charismatic renewal. Catholic charismatics did not generally teach that tongues were the initial evidence of Spirit baptism — a doctrine that sat uneasily with Catholic sacramental theology, which understood baptism and confirmation as the normative channels of the Spirit's gift. Instead, they spoke of a "release" or "renewal" of the Spirit already received in the sacraments. They maintained their commitment to the Mass, to the Marian doctrines, to papal authority, and to the full range of Catholic devotional practice. The renewal was not a Protestantization of Catholicism; it was an experiential intensification of an existing sacramental framework.

Pope Paul VI cautiously welcomed the movement, and subsequent popes — John Paul II, Benedict XVI, and Francis — have affirmed its place within the life of the church, while also warning against excesses. Today, the Catholic charismatic renewal claims over 120 million participants worldwide, making it one of the largest movements in the history of Catholicism.

## The Third Wave (1980s-Present)

The "Third Wave" is a term coined by C. Peter Wagner, a former professor at Fuller Theological Seminary's School of World Mission, to describe a movement of Christians who practice charismatic gifts (healing, prophecy, spiritual warfare) without identifying as either Pentecostal or charismatic. Third Wave theology emphasizes "signs and wonders" as normative for Christian ministry, and it tends to be less interested in the doctrine of Spirit baptism (the defining concern of classical Pentecostalism) and more interested in the practical exercise of spiritual power.

The Vineyard movement, founded by John Wimber in the early 1980s, was the most influential institutional expression of the Third Wave. Wimber, a former musician and church growth consultant, combined Reformed evangelical theology with an openness to the gifts of the Spirit that he called "power evangelism." Vineyard worship — intimate, emotionally intense, focused on personal encounter with God — became the template for contemporary worship in evangelical churches worldwide, whether or not those churches identified as charismatic.

The Third Wave also produced the controversial "Toronto Blessing" (1994) and the Brownsville Revival (1995), both characterized by unusual physical manifestations — "holy laughter," falling, shaking, animal sounds — that deeply divided the evangelical world. Supporters saw these manifestations as evidence of the Spirit's overwhelming presence. Critics saw them as emotional excess, psychological manipulation, or worse. The debates revealed a fault line within evangelical Christianity between those who regarded experiential phenomena as inherently suspicious and those who regarded the absence of experiential phenomena as evidence of spiritual deadness.

## Cessationism vs. Continuationism

The theological debate behind the charismatic movement is, at its core, a debate about whether the miraculous gifts described in the New Testament — tongues, prophecy, healing, miracles — continue to operate in the church today or ceased with the death of the apostles and the completion of the New Testament canon.

Cessationism — the view that the miraculous gifts ceased — has been the dominant position in Reformed and confessional Protestant theology since the Reformation. Its most influential modern articulation is Benjamin Warfield's *Counterfeit Miracles* (1918), which argued that miracles served as the credentials of the apostles and were no longer necessary once the apostolic testimony was inscripturated in the New Testament. John MacArthur's *Strange Fire* (2013) represented a more combative version of the same argument, accusing the charismatic movement of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.

Continuationism — the view that all the gifts continue — argues that there is no biblical warrant for a cessation of any spiritual gift. The New Testament nowhere teaches that the gifts will cease before the return of Christ. Paul's statement that tongues "will cease" and prophecy "will pass away" (1 Corinthians 13:8) is set in the context of the coming of "the perfect" (1 Corinthians 13:10), which continuationists identify not with the completion of the canon but with the return of Christ and the full consummation of the kingdom.

A significant middle position has emerged in recent decades, sometimes called "open but cautious" — the view that the gifts have not necessarily ceased but that their contemporary manifestations should be evaluated with rigorous biblical and theological discernment. This position, associated with scholars like D.A. Carson and Sam Storms, accepts the theoretical possibility of continued miraculous gifts while maintaining a high bar for their authentication.

## What the Movement Contributed

The charismatic movement's contributions to global Christianity are substantial and should be acknowledged even by those who disagree with its theological claims. First, it recovered the experiential dimension of faith in traditions that had become arid and intellectualized. The mainline Protestant churches of the mid-twentieth century were, in many cases, so focused on theological precision and social respectability that they had lost the capacity to speak of — or expect — a living encounter with God. The charismatic renewal reminded these churches that Christianity is not merely a system of beliefs but a relationship with a living person, and that the Holy Spirit is not merely a doctrine but a presence.

Second, the movement democratized ministry. Classical Pentecostalism's insistence that the Spirit's gifts are available to all believers — regardless of education, ordination, gender, or race — was a genuinely radical claim with practical consequences. It empowered lay people, elevated women in ministry (many early Pentecostal denominations ordained women long before mainline Protestants did), and created space for leadership from the margins of society.

Third, the charismatic movement has been the primary engine of Christian growth in the Global South. The explosive growth of Christianity in sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and East Asia over the past century has been overwhelmingly Pentecostal and charismatic in character. Philip Jenkins's observation that the "typical" Christian in the twenty-first century is not a European or American churchgoer but an African or Latin American Pentecostal is one of the most important demographic facts about contemporary Christianity.

## What the Movement Risks

The charismatic movement's vulnerabilities are as significant as its strengths, and honesty requires naming them. The first risk is *anti-intellectualism*. The emphasis on experience over doctrine, on encounter over analysis, on the Spirit's leading over theological education, has in many contexts produced a Christianity that is emotionally vibrant but theologically shallow. When "God told me" becomes a substitute for careful biblical exegesis, the result is a faith that is vulnerable to every wind of doctrine.

The second risk is *authoritarianism*. The charismatic movement's emphasis on prophetic authority — the claim that specific individuals can receive and communicate direct messages from God — creates a structural vulnerability to spiritual abuse. When a pastor or prophet claims to speak with divine authority, dissent becomes not merely disagreement but rebellion against God. The history of the charismatic movement is littered with leaders who used claims of prophetic authority to control their followers, suppress criticism, and shield themselves from accountability.

The third risk is *emotional manipulation*. The worship practices of charismatic churches — extended singing, repetitive musical patterns, high emotional intensity, altar calls, prayers for healing — can produce genuine spiritual encounters, but they can also produce manufactured emotional experiences that are mistaken for the work of the Spirit. The line between the two is not always easy to discern, and the charismatic movement has not always been careful about discerning it.

## The New Apostolic Reformation

The most controversial development within the charismatic world in recent decades is the New Apostolic Reformation (NAR) — a loosely organized movement that teaches that God is restoring the offices of apostle and prophet to the contemporary church, and that these new apostles and prophets have authority to direct the church and to influence the political and cultural direction of nations. The movement's leading figures — C. Peter Wagner (who coined the term before his death in 2016), Che Ahn, Bill Johnson, Mike Bickle, and others — teach that the church is entering a new era of spiritual power in which believers will exercise dominion over every sphere of society: government, business, education, media, arts, family, and religion.

The NAR has drawn sharp criticism from both cessationists and mainstream charismatics. Its theology of apostolic authority — which effectively places certain individuals above the accountability structures of the local church — creates obvious potential for abuse. Its "dominion theology" — the teaching that Christians are called to take control of societal institutions before Christ's return — represents a significant departure from the eschatological theology of classical Pentecostalism, which was premillennial and generally apolitical, expecting the world to grow worse before Christ's return rather than better.

The intersection of NAR theology with American political movements — particularly its involvement in the events surrounding the 2020 presidential election and its aftermath — has brought the movement unprecedented public scrutiny. Self-identified prophets within the NAR prophesied specific political outcomes that did not occur, generating a crisis of credibility that the movement has not fully reckoned with. The episode revealed the dangers of combining charismatic authority claims with political activism — a combination that can produce a form of Christianity that is impervious to correction, because its leaders claim to speak for God and its followers have been conditioned to regard skepticism as a lack of faith.

The charismatic movement, in all its waves and expressions, represents one of the most consequential developments in the history of Christianity. Its best impulses — the recovery of spiritual experience, the empowerment of the laity, the expectation that God acts in the present tense — are genuine gifts to the church. Its worst impulses — authoritarianism, anti-intellectualism, the confusion of emotional intensity with spiritual depth — are genuine dangers. The movement cannot be dismissed, and it cannot be embraced uncritically. It can only be engaged with the kind of careful, biblically grounded, theologically informed discernment that the best of the charismatic tradition itself calls for — the discernment of spirits, exercised not in fear but in love, and not in hostility but in hope for the church's faithfulness to the God who is, as the charismatics never tire of reminding us, still speaking.

chapters.title: The Council of Nicaea: What Was Actually Decided in 325
chapters.summary: Nicaea did not invent the divinity of Jesus or pick the books of the Bible. What it actually did still decides what you believe about your own salvation.
chapters.body:
Most of what people think they know about the Council of Nicaea, they learned from a novel. The story, repeated until it feels like common knowledge, is that in the year 325 the emperor Constantine gathered the bishops, held a vote, and invented the divinity of Jesus, and that the same council decided which books would go in the Bible, the whole thing a political maneuver to consolidate imperial power. Almost every piece of that is false. What actually happened is harder, and more interesting, and it still decides things you believe about your own salvation.

Nicaea did not settle the canon of Scripture. No book was added or burned there. The legend that the council fixed the New Testament and suppressed the rejected gospels appears in no record of the proceedings, and even skeptical historians of early Christianity grant that the canon was simply not the council's business (Ehrman 2003). And Nicaea did not invent the divinity of Christ. Christians had been worshipping Jesus as Lord, singing to him as God, baptizing in his name, and dying rather than burn incense to Caesar for nearly three centuries before any emperor convened anything. You do not need a council to command you to worship someone you are already willing to be executed for refusing to deny.

So what was the actual fight. A presbyter in Alexandria named Arius taught that the Son, though the first and highest of all beings, was a creature, made by the Father out of nothing before time began, so that, in his famous slogan, there was when the Son was not. The bishop Alexander and his young deacon Athanasius answered that the Son is eternally begotten, not made, of the same being as the Father. The entire conflict turned on one question. Is Jesus God in the full sense, or the greatest of God's creatures. The combatants fought over the same texts, John's claim that in the beginning the Word was with God and the Word was God (John 1:1 ESV), and Paul's that the Son is the firstborn of all creation, which Arius read as created and Athanasius read as heir and head over creation.

Steel-man the skeptic, because the surface facts give him plenty to work with. Constantine did convene the council and did want unity in his fracturing empire. The politics were real and often sordid. The decisive term the council chose, homoousios, of the same being, was not found in the Bible, and its absence troubled even some who were no friends of Arius. And the controversy did not end at Nicaea. It raged for the rest of the century, and Athanasius was driven into exile five separate times, once under an emperor who had swung to the Arian side. A person looking only at the imperial machinery could be forgiven for mistaking the whole thing for politics.

But the substance was not invented, and the vote was not close. Of roughly three hundred bishops present, all but two signed the creed, and many of them carried in their own bodies the scars of the persecutions that had ended barely a decade earlier. These were not imperial functionaries. They were survivors of torture being asked by a brand-new and not-yet-baptized Christian emperor to settle a question the church had raised itself. They drew the line at of one being with the Father because they saw what Arius's tidy solution destroyed. Athanasius made the stakes plain. Only God can save. If the one on the cross is a creature, then a creature is our savior, and we are worshipping someone less than God, which is idolatry, and worse, a creature cannot join us to a God he is not (Athanasius 2011).

The modern historians have shown how far the old cynical story falls short. Lewis Ayres argues that Nicaea was a genuine stage in theological development, the church slowly working out the grammar of what it had always done in worship, not a foreign idea stamped onto simple faith by an emperor (Ayres 2004). Jaroslav Pelikan traced the same long development and showed that the creed did not break with the worship of the earlier church but defended it, naming in formal language the divine Christ the church had confessed from the beginning (Pelikan 1971). That is the reframe the novel misses entirely. The creed did not impose philosophy on a Galilean carpenter. It protected the carpenter, the plain confession that Jesus is Lord, from a sophisticated philosophical attempt to shrink him into a demigod.

And it still matters, because a Christ who is merely the highest creature is a Christ who cannot save, and a Christianity built on him is a religion of admiring a fine example, which is to say a religion of works, you straining to follow a hero who cannot reach back. The entire weight of grace hangs on the one word the bishops fought for. If the one bleeding on the cross is God himself bearing what we owed, that is salvation. If he is a creature God dispatched to bear it, that is cosmic injustice with a halo. Everything you actually believe about whether you can be rescued is hiding inside that word.

The bishops at Nicaea were not defending their power. Most of them had just finished losing everything for refusing to deny the very thing the council affirmed. They handed the church one word it could not read straight off the surface of the Bible but could not live without, and they were right to bleed for it. The novel got the drama right and the facts wrong. The truth was less of a conspiracy and more of a confession, signed by men who had already proven what their confession was worth.

### Works Cited

Athanasius. 2011. On the Incarnation. Translated by John Behr. Yonkers, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press.

Ayres, Lewis. 2004. Nicaea and Its Legacy. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Ehrman, Bart D. 2003. Lost Christianities. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Pelikan, Jaroslav. 1971. The Christian Tradition, Volume 1. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.

chapters.title: The Crusades: What Actually Happened
chapters.summary: The Crusades are the favorite club used against the faith. The honest history is worse than the cliche, and its deepest critique is Christian, not secular.
chapters.body:
The Crusades are the club. Raise the violence of religion in any argument and they arrive within a sentence, offered as the proof that faith makes people kill. The honest history is worse than the cliche and also more complicated than it, and a Christianity that cannot tell the truth about its own worst chapters has no business asking anyone to trust it about anything.

So tell the truth. The First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099, and the soldiers massacred the city, Muslims and Jews together, in a slaughter the chroniclers describe with horror and pride in the same sentence. On the way there, in 1096, crusaders in the Rhineland turned on the Jewish communities and murdered thousands, among the first great pogroms of European history, carried out by men wearing the cross. And the Fourth Crusade, in 1204, never reached a Muslim army at all. It sacked Constantinople, the greatest Christian city in the world, and Christians looted and desecrated the churches of other Christians. None of this can be explained away, and the attempt to explain it away is itself a second offense.

Steel-man the critic fully. The argument made by Christopher Hitchens and Sam Harris is that here is religion doing exactly what religion does, sanctifying slaughter with the name of God, and that the Crusades are not an aberration but a revelation of what belief licenses (Hitchens 2007). Give it its weight. The atrocities were real, they were vast, and they were done explicitly in the name of Christ with the promise of heaven attached. A believer who shrugs that off has not reckoned with it.

Now the other correction, because the cartoon is false in the opposite direction. The popular picture of the Crusades as unprovoked Western colonial aggression against a peaceful East is bad history. The historians, Thomas Madden and Christopher Tyerman among them, point out that the Crusades came after four centuries of conquest that had taken three-quarters of the formerly Christian world, including the Holy Land itself, and that the First Crusade was called in answer to an appeal from the Christian East against advancing armies (Madden 2005). The medieval crusader was not a modern colonialist. Most went bankrupt going, and many went believing they were defending their brothers and reclaiming stolen ground. The history is a tangle of real grievance and real horror, and both are true at once.

But here is the reversal that neither the atheist nor the defensive apologist wants to hear. The Crusades do not indict Christianity by being too Christian. They indict it by being a betrayal of Christianity, the photographic negative of its own Lord. On the night he was arrested, Peter drew a sword to defend him, the one moment in the Gospels a disciple takes up arms for Jesus, and Jesus stopped him cold. Put your sword back into its place, he said, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52 ESV). Standing before Pilate he said that his kingdom was not of this world, and that if it were, his servants would fight (John 18:36). The whole logic of the cross is a king who conquers by dying rather than by killing, who refuses the legions he could have called down. Measure the Crusades against that and they are not the fruit of the faith. They are its inversion.

Which means the most devastating critique of the Crusades is not the atheist's. It is the Christian one. The atheist says religion made them violent. The gospel says they abandoned the religion the moment they raised a sword in its name, because the founder of it went unarmed to his own execution and told his followers the world would know them by their love and not by their conquests. You cannot use the Crusades to refute a faith whose Lord and whose earliest martyrs died precisely by refusing to do what the crusaders did.

It is easy to condemn men dead a thousand years. The harder thing is to notice that the crusading impulse, the certainty that God's cause can be advanced by force and that our enemies are therefore his, did not die in the Middle Ages. It only traded the sword for other weapons, the culture war waged as though it were a holy war, the opponent to be crushed rather than the neighbor to be loved. We did this. Some version of we keeps doing it.

The church should not flinch from the Crusades, and it should not excuse them. It should own them, and then it should say the one thing that is both true and damning. They were done in the name of a Lord who would have stopped them, who did stop Peter, who chose the cross over the sword and asked his people to do the same. The kingdom of God has never once advanced by killing for him. It has only ever advanced by people willing to die for him. The crusaders forgot which one they were called to. So, often, do we.

### Works Cited

Hitchens, Christopher. 2007. God Is Not Great. New York: Twelve.

Madden, Thomas F. 2005. The New Concise History of the Crusades. Lanham, MD: Rowman and Littlefield.

Tyerman, Christopher. 2006. God's War: A New History of the Crusades. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press.

chapters.title: The Great Awakenings and the Making of American Faith
chapters.summary: American Christianity was born in revival. That fire gave it a faith of the heart, and it also taught it to trust feeling over the church. We live in both.
chapters.body:
American Christianity was born in fire, and the fire left a mark that is both its genius and its wound.

Twice the country was swept by mass revival, and both times it changed not only how many Americans believed but what believing was. The First Great Awakening broke out in the 1730s and 1740s, when Jonathan Edwards preached and a young Anglican named George Whitefield crossed the colonies drawing crowds of thousands in open fields, and people wept and collapsed and were converted where they stood.
